blocks.content: Favour composition over inheritance" is one of the most repeated principles in software design straight from the Gang of Four. But what does it actually mean, when do you use it, and why is it often better than inheritance? This topic answers all of that with clear examples.
1. What is Composition?
Composition means building a class by containing instances of other classes instead of inheriting from them. Rather than saying "A is a B," you say "A has a B."
The object being composed delegates specific behaviour to the objects it contains. If Car needs an engine, instead of extending Engine, it holds an Engine.

ANALOGY: A COMPUTER

A computer is not a CPU, not a keyboard, not a screen. A computer has a CPU, has a keyboard, has a screen. Each component is its own thing, interchangeable, and independently upgradeable. You can swap the keyboard without touching the CPU. That's composition building something powerful by assembling capable parts.
blocks.title: Note

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-content-images/1781076236886-181653683.png
This diagram represents a Car and the components it is built from. The Car class contains an Engine, a Transmission, and Brakes.
Instead of implementing all functionality itself, the car relies on these specialized components to perform different tasks.
When the car needs to start, it uses the Engine. When the driver changes gears, the car delegates that operation to the Transmission.
Similarly, when the car needs to slow down or stop, it uses the Brakes. In other words, the car is composed of smaller objects that work together to provide the complete functionality of a vehicle.
The filled diamond symbol below the Car class represents Composition, which is a strong "has-a" relationship.

It means that the Engine, Transmission, and Brakes belong to the Car and are part of its lifecycle. If the Car is destroyed, these components are destroyed as well because they cannot meaningfully exist independently of the Car.
In simple terms, this diagram shows that a Car has an Engine, a Transmission, and Brakes, and it uses these internal components to perform actions such as starting, stopping, and shifting gears.
This is a classic example of Composition in Object-Oriented Design.
2. Composition vs Inheritance
Both are ways to reuse code. The difference is how the relationship is expressed and what it costs you.
3. Why "Has-A" is Often Better Than "Is-A"
The "is-a" test for inheritance sounds logical: a Dog is an Animal, so Dog extends Animal makes sense. But "is-a" relationships in code are much more restrictive than in natural language.

When you say "Dog is-a Animal" in Java, you're saying Dog can be used anywhere Animal is expected, forever, with all of Animal's behaviour. That's a permanent, deep coupling that's hard to escape later.

ANALOGY: A SWISS ARMY KNIFE VS A TOOLBOX

A Swiss Army knife inherits every blade you can't remove the corkscrew if you never need it. You're stuck with the full package. 

A toolbox composes tools you pick exactly what you need for each job, swap tools in and out, and your hammer doesn't know anything about your screwdriver. Composition gives you the toolbox model.
blocks.title: Note

blocks.content: The classic example from the Gang of Four book:
StackextendingVector. A Stack is not really a Vector a Stack shouldn't exposeinsertElementAt()orget(index).
But by inheriting Vector, Java's original Stack class exposed all of those methods, making it easy to break the stack contract. Composition would have been correct:
Stackhasa Vector internally, but only exposespush(),pop(), andpeek().
1. Inheritance: Exposes Everything From Parent, Even What Should Not Be Accessible
In the first example, Stack inherits from Vector. Because of inheritance, Stack automatically gets all methods of Vector, including operations like add(index, element) and get(index).
This is a problem because users can insert elements anywhere in the stack, breaking the LIFO (Last In, First Out) behavior that a stack should enforce.

codes.python:
class Stack(list):
    # inherits insert(index, value), pop(index), __getitem__(index)...
    # now callers can bypass the stack contract entirely
    pass


if __name__ == "__main__":
    stack = Stack()
    stack.append(0)
    stack.append(1)
    stack.append(2)
    stack.insert(0, 42)   # inserts at the bottom, not how a stack should work!
    print(stack)

blocks.content: 2. Composition: Exposes Only What Makes Sense for a Stack

In the second example, Stack contains a Deque internally instead of inheriting from it. The stack only exposes methods that make sense, such as push(), pop(), and peek(). Users cannot access low-level operations that would break the stack's behavior, so the stack remains safe and easier to maintain.
Key Idea: Inheritance exposes everything from the parent class, while Composition exposes only what is needed. That's why composition is often preferred over inheritance.
4. Problems with Deep Inheritance
Inheritance seems like a great idea for reuse until the hierarchy grows. Then the problems compound.

["Problem 1: The fragile base class problem
"]
items: Problem 1: The fragile base class problem

blocks.content: When you change a parent class, you potentially break every child class even ones you didn't know about. The parent and all its descendants are coupled together. A "safe" change to the parent can silently break a grandchild class in a way that only shows up at runtime.

["Problem 2: The gorilla-banana problem
"]

The problem with object-oriented languages is they've got all this implicit environment that they carry around with them. You wanted a banana but what you got was a gorilla holding the banana and the entire jungle." When you inherit from a class to get one method, you get everything else that class carries whether you want it or not.

["Problem 3: Inflexibility at runtime
"]
Inheritance is decided at compile time. You can't change what a Dog inherits while the program is running. Composition lets you swap behaviours dynamically.

["Problem 4: Broken \"is-a\" in practice
"]
SOUNDS LIKE "IS-A" BUT BREAKS LISKOV SUBSTITUTION
A Square geometrically is a Rectangle. But in code,Square extends Rectangleviolates Liskov Substitution aSquarecannot be safely used everywhere aRectangleis expected.
Composition would be cleaner: bothSquareandRectangleimplement aShapeinterface separately.
5. Composition in Practice
Let's see composition replace inheritance with a real example a notification system that can send emails, SMS, and push notifications.
1. With inheritance ( rigid and limiting )

In the inheritance approach, each notification type becomes a separate class such asEmailNotifier,SmsNotifier, andPushNotifier. This works fine until a user wants multiple notification methods, like Email + SMS. Now you need a new class such asEmailAndSmsNotifier.
If you later want Email + SMS + Push, you need another class. The number of classes keeps growing, making the design rigid and hard to maintain.
2. With composition (mix any combination freely)
In the composition approach, each notification channel (Email,SMS,Push) is a separate component.
TheNotifiersimply contains a list of channels and sends the message through all of them. If a user wants Email only, add the Email channel.
If they want Email + SMS + Push, just combine those channels. No new classes are needed.
6. Composition with Interfaces ( The Power Move )
blocks.text: 6. Composition with Interfaces ( The Power Move )

blocks.content: Composition becomes most powerful when combined with interfaces. You define what something can do (the interface) and then plug in how it does it (the implementation) swappable at any time.
This is the Strategy pattern one of the most useful design patterns and it's pure composition.
WHY THIS IS SO POWERFUL
Adding a new sorting algorithm requires zero changes to DataSorter. You just write a new class that implements SortStrategy.
Open-Closed Principle satisfied open for extension (new strategies), closed for modification (DataSorter unchanged). This is the power of composition + interfaces.
7. Real-World Example::Payment System
A payment system needs to support multiple payment methods: credit card, UPI, wallet, net banking.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-content-images/1781076238298-58094976.png
New methods get added regularly. Inheritance makes this painful; composition makes it clean.
The Order class does not directly know how to process a credit card payment or a UPI payment.
Instead, it contains a PaymentMethod object. This means the order can work with any payment method that follows the PaymentMethod interface.
For example, if the customer chooses a credit card, the order uses CreditCardPayment.
If the customer chooses UPI, the order uses UpiPayment. The checkout logic inside Order remains exactly the same.
The biggest advantage is flexibility. If a new payment method such as Wallet, PayPal, or Net Banking is added later, you simply create a new class that implements PaymentMethod.
The Order class does not need any modification.
In simple words, Order HAS-A PaymentMethod, and that payment method can be swapped at runtime. This makes the system easy to extend and maintain.
8. When Inheritance is the Right Choice
blocks.text: 8. When Inheritance is the Right Choice

blocks.content: Composition is usually better but inheritance has legitimate uses. The key question is: does the "is-a" relationship hold up under substitution?
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-content-images/1781076238461-404659255.png
THE LISKOV TEST

Before using inheritance, ask: "Can I replace every use of the parent with an instance of the child without breaking anything?" If yes inheritance is safe. If no use composition or let both implement a shared interface.
9. Common Mistakes

["Mistake 1: Inheriting just to reuse one method
"]
items: Mistake 1: Inheriting just to reuse one method

blocks.content: Extending a class just to get one useful method drags in everything else all the fields, all the other methods, all the coupling. Compose instead: extract that one method into an interface and inject it.
1. INHERITING LOGGER JUST TO GET LOG()
2. INJECT THE LOGGER AS A DEPENDENCY

["Mistake 2: Deep inheritance chains
"]

A → B → C → D → E any change in A ripples through everything. At 4+ levels deep, no one can reason about what a subclass actually does without reading the entire chain. Flatten the hierarchy. If subclasses share behaviour, extract it into a composed component.

["Mistake 3: Overriding to break parent behaviour
"]
items: Mistake 3: Overriding to break parent behaviour

blocks.content: If a subclass overrides a method to do nothing, or to throw an exception for an operation the parent supports, it's violating Liskov Substitution. The subclass is no longer truly "is-a" the parent. Composition is the fix.

["Mistake 4: Using composition but still coupling tightly
"]
items: Mistake 4: Using composition but still coupling tightly

blocks.content: Composing concrete classes instead of interfaces couples you to the implementation. Always compose against interfaces the actual class injected can change without touching the containing class.
1. COMPOSED AGAINST A CONCRETE CLASS: TIGHTLY COUPLED
2. COMPOSED AGAINST AN INTERFACE: LOOSELY COUPLED
10. Summary

Inheritance gives you tight coupling and a rigid hierarchy.","Inheritance is permanent and decided at compile time. Inject the dependency instead. Don't build deep chains (A→B→C→D) flatten with composition.","\"Favour composition over inheritance\" Gang of Four, 1994. items: Composition = building a class by containing instances of other classes. "A has-a B" rather than "A is-a B".
Composition gives you loose coupling, swappable parts, runtime flexibility, and independent testability. Inheritance gives you tight coupling and a rigid hierarchy.
Inheritance is permanent and decided at compile time. Composition can change at runtime swap an implementation without changing the containing class.
The fragile base class problem: changing a parent breaks all its children. Composition avoids this parts only know about their own interface.
Compose against interfaces, not concrete classes. This gives you all the flexibility of composition with the ability to swap implementations.
The Strategy pattern is composition in its purest form define behaviour as an interface, inject the implementation, swap at will.
Inheritance is right when the "is-a" relationship holds under Liskov Substitution every child can substitute its parent without breaking anything.
Don't inherit just to reuse one method. Inject the dependency instead. Don't build deep chains (A→B→C→D) flatten with composition.
"Favour composition over inheritance" Gang of Four, 1994. Still the most useful single design principle in OOP.
